subject: axolotl
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: axolotl with frilly pink gills.
Style: chibi.

spec.name: Chibi Axolotl
spec.description: A chubby chibi axolotl: a pink leucistic body with an oversized head, glossy black eyes, a wide smile, stubby limbs, a finned tail and six frilly hot-pink gill plumes.
spec.layout: Real axolotl scale (about 0.42 m nose to tail tip), chibi proportions. The animal lies flat on the floor in a neutral T-pose-like rest: head forward, body behind it, tail straight back along -Z, limbs splayed sideways with fingers fanned, and gills spread outward like a fan. Z runs from the snout at +0.17 to the tail tip at -0.255. The head is about 40% of the body length and about 0.16 wide, a broad, flat, rounded wedge with a blunt rounded snout, puffy cheeks and a wide upturned smile whose corners tuck into the cheeks. Eyes are big glossy black beads on the top-front sides of the head, each with a big and a small white highlight, small pink brow bumps above them and rosy blush discs on the cheeks. The torso behind the head is a fat rounded sausage with a pale belly sector underneath and a darker pink back with a few rose freckles. A low frilled dorsal fin runs from the back of the head over the back and continues into the tail fin. The tail is a vertically flattened oval tube with a fin skirt above and below, tapering to a rounded tip. Four stubby legs: front legs have 4 fingers, hind legs 4 toes, all with rounded fat toe tips and a darker pad. Three gill plumes per side sprout from the back of the head at upper, middle and lower height. Each plume is a tapered stalk with two rows of curled, tapering filaments, shading from deep pink at the root to light pink at the tips. They fan up, out and slightly back (about +/-0.165 m out at the widest) and are the signature feature, built bold and dense. Everything is faceted low-poly in flat colours, with a chunky, bold and cute look. Details (eyes, highlights, freckles, blush, nostrils, toe pads) are small parts seated on the surfaces in their own colours.

parts.builds: The big chibi head on joints head and jaw, as a separate upper head and lower jaw. Upper head: a broad flat rounded skull (squashed sphere or loft about 0.15 wide, 0.1 tall, 0.14 long) with a blunt rounded snout in skin pink, a slightly darker skinBack top cap, puffy cheek bulges, and two tiny nostril dimples in nostril colour at nostrilTop (x +/-0.012). Lower jaw on joint jaw: a smaller rounded wedge that closes under the upper head and ends at the chin at z 0.16, in skin with a pale belly-coloured underside. Mouth: a wide smile line in mouthLine, a thin swept tube along the lip seam between the jaws with corners curling up into the cheeks near cheekL/cheekR, plus a dark mouthInside sliver and a small tongue in tongue colour on the jaw, visible only as a hint. Eyes: big glossy beads (radius about 0.017) at eyeL/eyeR in eye colour with an eyeRing rim disc behind each, one big and one small eyeShine highlight sphere seated on the front-upper surface, and a small brow bump in brow colour above each eye. Rosy blush discs in blush colour on the cheeks at cheekL/cheekR facing outward and forward. A few freckle dots in freckle colour on the forehead. The back of the head tapers into the body at neckJoin and headBack, leaving room for the gill roots, which sit on the head's back sides. Nothing may sit in front of the face.
parts.attaches: Back of the head overlaps the body front at neckJoin and headBack. Gill stalks root at the gill*Root mounts on the rear flanks of this head. Dorsal fin begins at dorsalStart on the top rear of the head.

parts.builds: The fat rounded torso from neckJoin (z 0.07, tucked inside the head) back to the tail root at z -0.075, riding joints hips and chest. A loft or sweep with a slightly oval section about 0.1 wide and 0.085 tall, bellying wider at the chest, in skin pink with a skinBack top sector and a belly-coloured pale underside sector (use sweep sectors or loft colours). Belly sits at about y 0.005. A frilled low dorsal fin along the spine from dorsalStart to hipsTop: a thin membrane or extruded ripple fin in fin colour with a finEdge rim and small finRay ridge parts, rising about 0.012 to 0.015 m above the back. Small round freckle spots in freckle colour scattered over the back and sides, about 14 to 20 spots, seated on the surface. Shoulder and hip bulges in skin where the limbs attach, at shoulderL/R and hipL/R, small soft rounded mounds. Optionally a tiny cloaca bump on the underside near z -0.07.
parts.attaches: Front end tucks into the head at neckJoin. The rear end joins the tail at tailRoot (radius matches the tail start, about 0.036 wide by 0.04 tall). The dorsal fin continues into the tail fin at hipsTop. Limb roots seat on shoulderL/R and hipL/R.

parts.builds: The axolotl tail on joints tail1 to tail4, running straight back along -Z from tailRoot to tailTip at z -0.255. A smooth-skinned sweep with a vertically flattened oval section (about 0.034 wide by 0.04 tall at the root, tapering to a rounded tip about 0.006 wide), in skin pink with a pale belly sector underneath. A tall tail fin: a membrane or extruded skirt along the top and the bottom edge of the tube, in fin colour with a finEdge rim line along the outer edge, and fine finRay lines (thin sweeps or small parts) fanning across the fin. Fin height is about 0.03 above and about 0.02 below at the root, narrowing smoothly to the tip, and it continues the dorsal fin at hipsTop. A few freckle dots along the tail sides. Rounded, chunky and cute, and it bends smoothly with the chain.
parts.attaches: Starts at tailRoot, meeting the torso end. The top fin joins the dorsal fin at hipsTop. The tip is at tailTip.

parts.builds: Four stubby chibi legs, mirrored left and right, on the arm chains (shoulderL/R, elbowL/R, wristL/R) and the leg chains (hipL/R, kneeL/R, ankleL/R). Each limb is a fat tapered sweep (about 0.016 radius at the root to 0.011 at the wrist) in skin pink, with a rounded joint cap at the shoulder or hip where it meets the body. The hands sit on the floor at about y 0.012 and the feet likewise, so the lowest points touch y 0. Each hand is a flat paddle with 4 fingers fanned apart forward and outward; each foot is the same with 4 toes (splayed). Each digit is a short tapered rod with a round fat tip in toe colour, with a small toePad dot on the underside of each tip. Add a rounded palm or sole disc. The builder creates the digit joints itself with role digit and group limbs, named fingerL1 to fingerL4 and fingerR1 to fingerR4 on wristL/wristR, and toeL1 to toeL4 and toeR1 to toeR4 on ankleL/ankleR, each parented to its wrist or ankle joint. The digits splay in a fan about 70 degrees wide, pointing forward and outward, each about 0.03 long. Front limbs are slightly bigger than the hind limbs. A couple of freckle dots on each upper limb.
parts.attaches: Roots at shoulderL/R and hipL/R on the sides of the body; each limb root is buried slightly inside the torso. Feet and hands rest on the floor.

parts.builds: The signature frilly gills: three plumes per side (top, mid, low) on the chains gillTopL1/2, gillMidL1/2, gillLowL1/2 and the mirrored R chains (group gills, role fan). Each plume is a tapered stalk sweep along its joints, thick at the root (radius about 0.009) and thinning to about 0.004, in gillStalk colour, with a rounded gillRoot collar sphere where it meets the head at the gill*Root mounts. Along each stalk, filaments grow on both sides in two rows, 7 to 9 per side per plume. Each filament is a thin curved tapered sweep or spike (about 0.03 to 0.05 long near the middle, shorter near the tip), splayed 40 to 60 degrees off the stalk and curling slightly upward and back, coloured root to tip with gillMid and gillTip (bases in gillRoot or gillMid, tips in gillTip), with a tiny round bulb at each filament tip. Each stalk ends in a bunch of 3 short filaments. Bold overlapping fans, dense and fluffy, nothing thin enough to vanish. Top plumes reach up to about y 0.165, mid plumes spread widest to x +/-0.165, low plumes droop outward at about y 0.03. Make left and right match in mirror. Filaments ride the gill joint nearest their stalk point. Keep the gills clear of the face (they are behind the eyes, z at or behind about 0.05).
parts.attaches: Plume roots sit on the rear flanks of the head at gillTopRootL/R, gillMidRootL/R and gillLowRootL/R, which are slightly inside the head surface so they seat in it.

calls.reasoning:
I'm sketching the proportions for a chibi axolotl with frilly pink gills, thinking through realistic scale versus the exaggerated big-head chibi style, settling on roughly 0.36 wide by 0.17 tall by 0.42 long for the body dimensions.

Now I'm laying out the skeleton structure: placing hips as the root joint with a spine chain leading to the chest, then a head joint, a jaw hinge for the mouth, and a tail chain extending backward with multiple segments for flexible movement.

Still working out front and hind leg joint chains...

I'll let the limb builder generate digit joints itself with naming conventions like fingerFL1-4 for front hands and toe joints for hind feet, rather than pre-listing every one for determinism — simpler and conflicts should be minimal. For gills, I'm planning three branching stalks per side with frilly filaments, each needing its own parent joint chain.

Working through the gill joint placement now — positioning the stalk bases at the back-sides of the head and fanning them upper/middle/lower, trying to settle on clear naming like gillTopL, gillMidL, gillLowL so each chain's left/right and position is unambiguous.

Now I'm shaping the head: a wide, flat, rounded axolotl head with big chibi-style eyes on the top-front sides and a wide smiling mouth, sized larger than the body for the cute proportions. I'm setting the head bounding box and jaw position near the floor, then scaling the body down smaller in comparison to the oversized head.

For the body, I'm giving it a sagging belly resting on the floor and splitting the model into parts: a head group (skull, snout, jaws, eyes, cheeks, mouth details, spots) at a 200-part budget with head/jaw joints, and a body group with torso, belly, dorsal fin crest, and speckles at 150 parts, plus a separate tail piece with its fin membrane.

Beyond that I'm adding gills (six stalks per side with filaments at 250 parts) and four limbs with digits at 170 parts, keeping the total under 900. I'm defining the tail's vertical flattened cross-section continuous with the dorsal fin, and setting up mount points like hipsTop, neckJoin, tailRoot, and shoulder/hip joints so the body and tail builders connect seamlessly.

Now I'm sweeping the torso geometry from the head junction back to where the tail begins, sizing the tail's oval cross-section and tip position. I'm also setting up the leucistic pink axolotl color palette—body pink, belly cream, hot pink gills, dark eyes, and blush tones.

Still placing coordinates...

Combining limb boxes into one shared bounding region, deciding which parts should rest exactly on the floor (limbs yes, head no), and sketching out shoulder-to-wrist joint positions so the leg reaches down naturally to foot level.

Now I'm laying out the hip-knee-ankle chain for the hind legs, then building the joint hierarchy: root hips, chest, head, and jaw, each with position offsets and spine direction, working toward placing the jaw hinge near the back of the head so it can open toward the chin.

Jaw gets its role assigned, then I'm chaining out the tail segments from hips through four tapering bones. I'm planning to predefine all joints with b.joint before using b.chain and b.sweep to build the actual limb parts, assigning roles like "arm" and "leg" to the shoulder and hind joints and setting each joint's direction to aim toward the next in the chain.

Now I'm computing the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joint positions and directions for the arms, mirroring the left side to negative x for the right, and moving on to the gill joints anchored relative to the head's back position.

Still placing gill joints...

Now I'm adding mount points for head, mouth corners, and eyes, then defining the chibi style overall: big head proportion, stubby limbs, glossy highlighted eyes, blush, smile, and fluffy gills made of tapered comb-like filaments along each stalk.

Working out the part budgets: gill filaments with gradient coloring and small bulb tips, then dividing the roughly 860-point budget across body, head, gills, limbs, and tail, with each builder owning specific sub-features like shoulder caps, cheeks, eye sockets, brow, and the simple smiling mouth.

I need to write buildLimbs using the Ctx, creating digit joints like fingerL1 parented under wrist, tagged with role digit and group limbs, following the naming convention the spec calls for even though it's a bit ambiguous whether names should start with "limbs" or match the finger pattern—I'll go with the finger-named approach the spec seems to intend.

I'm sweeping a smooth skin along a catmull path through the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joint positions, then positioning a flat palm disc at the wrist sized so its bottom edge sits right at the floor. For the digits, I'm fanning them out from the wrist at roughly a 70-degree spread, angled forward and outward for the left side.

Now I'm defining each digit joint as a child of the wrist, aimed along its fan direction, with a tapered rod geometry and a tip sphere plus small flattened toe pad underneath, sized so the lowest point grazes the floor.

I'm mirroring the digit setup across left and right sides by flipping the base direction's X sign, keeping the same fan-angle rotation about Y for both hands.

Hind toes get a slight 0.9 scale down. For the limbs, I'm defining tapered sweep geometry with front and hind radii, routing a smooth catmull-rom path through shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints, and capping each joint with a rounded sphere sized to blend into the torso.

I'll skip adding a pad on the palm since it'd be invisible anyway. For freckles, I'll place small flattened spheres onto points along the limb's sweep surface at a couple of t-values and angles, embedding them slightly into the surface for a natural look.

Now I'm working out the joint and digit structure: creating joints with parent references and roles, then building each digit as a capsule running from base to tip with a small sphere capping the end.

Still working out hand geometry...

Writing helper function for limbs...

I need to write the buildGills function using the existing joints (gillTopL1 and gillTopL2) to sweep a stalk shape along a path that starts at the mount root and passes through the second joint to the tip.

Still working out positions...

I'm computing root, mid-joint, and tip coordinates for three plumes (top, mid, low) on the left side, mirroring for the right side by negating x. I'll build each stalk's path with a catmull curve through the root, joint, and tip points, using the joint list for bone association, a tapered radius with round caps, and then add filament details branching off along the stalk using points sampled from the path.

Now I'm figuring out how to color the swept tube along its length with colored bands transitioning from root to tip (root, mid, tip colors), while keeping an eye on the total mesh/part budget across all six plumes with their filaments and bulbs.

Simplifying to two parts per filament—colored sweep plus tip bulb—and cutting to 6 stations with 2 filaments each plus 3 terminal gets me to roughly 15 filaments per plume, about 90 total, under 210 parts. I'll vary colour by position: root stations use gillRoot, mid stations gillMid, and all bulbs use gillTip.

Now I'm thinking about making each plume feel fluffier, feather-like. For each station I need a side vector perpendicular to the tangent that spreads filaments outward in two rows (roughly front/back), combined with an upward curl, so I'm working out how to define that side axis consistently along the curve.

Adding depth variation between rows with alternating z-offsets, then working out filament length tapering so they're shorter near the tip and root, and curving each filament with a quadratic bezier that bends upward and back from the stalk.

Sweeping each filament's radius from thicker at the base to thin at the tip with rounded caps, capping it with a small bulb sphere colored for the gill tip. Checking that the thickness feels proportional at this 0.4m model scale, settling around 0.0045m radius, then assigning bone weights so filaments near the stalk rig to the first joint and those further along the plume rig to the second joint.

I'm adjusting the tip position of the plume so the filament bulbs stay within the bounding box, shrinking the offset from J2 to avoid exceeding the y=0.17 ceiling.

Checking the mid and low plume positions similarly, keeping their tip offsets small so outward and downward splayed filaments don't cross the box edges.

Setting up the mirroring logic so left and right sides share joint positions with x-offsets flipped by side sign. Adding a small collar sphere at the gill root joint, and defining the stalk sweep geometry with tapered radii along the bone path.

For the filament direction, I'm computing a tangent-normal frame at each path point so each filament fans out at an angle from the stalk, alternating sides and rows, then layering in a z-offset per row to give the gills some vertical texture.

For the gill stations, I'm placing six of them along the path (t from 0.14 to 0.9), each with two filaments splaying in opposite directions, offsetting rows in z, and coloring filaments by index — early stations use the root/stalk color, later ones shift toward the mid and tip gill colors.

At the terminal tip I'm adding a small bunch of three filaments splayed around the direction vector, colored and bulbed toward the tip hue, with slight randomized length variation and using bezier sweeps with vector points, round caps, and modest sides for a smooth low-poly look, starting each sweep just inside the stalk surface.

Building the curved paths now, pulling root and mount points from the skeleton dictionary (mirroring left/right sides via sign on x), cloning vectors from joint positions so each filament bends naturally from root through a mid joint to its tip.

I'm working out the tail-building function, using the existing tail1-tail4 joints already positioned along the z-axis rather than creating a new chain, and sweeping geometry across that bone list to form the tail shape.

I'm defining a catmull-rom path through the joint positions, tapering the tube radius from wider near the root (rx 0.017, ry 0.02) down to narrow at the tip (rx 0.004, ry 0.006), while keeping the overlap with the torso box in mind and making sure the tube widths run consistently along world X regardless of the tail's backward direction.

Now I'm working out the dorsal fin membrane, building paired edge paths by sampling tube surface points and offsetting them upward by a tapering height function (starting around 0.03 at the root and shrinking toward the tip near the top of the tube).

Maybe the simplest robust approach is four membrane segments, each rigid to its own bone, splitting the fin at the joint z-positions so they share boundary points at rest pose—bending will crack slightly at joints but should be tolerable since the fin is thin. I'm weighing whether to instead try a smoother approach using point arrays for the edges.

Maybe slabs per segment with quad points could work, but I think I'll go with extrude per segment instead, defining a side-view outline with a frilled bump on the top edge, positioned at the base of each tube segment.

Now I'm defining helper functions for the fin's centerline and radius, computing the embedded root position inside the tube and the frill height above the tube's top surface at each z-coordinate.

Then top from u1→u0, keeping both ends vertical and ensuring top always exceeds base so segments don't self-intersect, with no smoothing on corners. I'm defining u as the negative z-coordinate so the outline's x values run positive along the tail, letting me place each fin segment by its z-range and start the dorsal fin near the hips around z=-0.07.

Now I'm working out the fin's y-profile as a near-linear interpolation across sampled z-points, then adjusting the tail tip so the rounded cap doesn't push past the bounding box, trimming the path end to -0.248 instead of -0.256. I'm setting up radius functions along the path length so I can compute rx and ry at any z by converting to a normalized fraction of the fin's total length.

I'm rethinking the fin rays to cut part count—spacing them wider (every 0.016 instead of 0.012) and using a single thin box piercing through the fin thickness rather than separate rods on each side, which roughly halves the budget to around 44 parts total.

Adding rim sweep geometry...

Still working out the outline geometry...

For the bottom fin I'm scalloping the boundary so valley points sit higher than the full-depth peaks, mirroring the top fin's taper. I'm also setting up fin coloring (pale belly sector, edge rims) and figuring out ray lines for both fins — placing rays at each peak with a backward lean so they fan out from the base toward the tip.

Tallying the part count now: roughly 32 ray segments across both fins, plus rims, fin bodies, tube, and a handful of freckles for around 65 total pieces. For the freckles, I'm planning to stick small sphere geometries onto the tube surface using its sweep frame to get accurate positions along the body.

Working out the clockwise angle convention is tricky since the viewer faces -Z, so I'm reasoning through which side corresponds to 90 degrees and landing on the -X side as the clockwise-from-up direction, then picking symmetric angle ranges on both sides for the freckle placement. I'm flattening the freckle spheres slightly with a non-uniform scale so they read as blotches rather than bumps, distributing roughly a dozen of them across the back sides at varying positions along the tube.

For the tail geometry itself, I'm configuring the sweep's cross-section with 10 sides and setting color sectors so the belly region and back region get distinct skin tones, then assembling the sweep from the chain of tail joint positions, checking that the path's starting point lines up sensibly with the first joint.

Now I'm working out the vertical offset of the path along its length using a piecewise linear helper between sampled z and y points, and mapping each tail segment to its corresponding joint boundary.

Still defining tail geometry...

I'll go with N=4 segments and place rays at interior sample points, 12 per fin total, then extrude the outline into a thin fin shape with slight lean and bevel for a finished edge.

Still defining ray geometry...

Pulling colors from the palette object for skin, belly, fin, fin edge, fin ray, and freckles.

I'm planning the torso construction, lofting the body from the chest region back toward the tail root with a box shape sized to fit between the existing hip and chest joints.

Working out the geometry, I think a sweep approach anchored to the hip and chest joints makes more sense than a loft, with a path curving from rear to front and a radius function tapering width between the tail and front sections.

Working out the front end taper — using flat caps near the head since it'll be hidden there anyway, then defining a radius function that tapers from narrow at the rear to wider through the body.

Setting the belly center and radius so top and bottom bounds stay consistent, and picking 12 sides for a nicer low-poly blob silhouette. I'm defining the body path as a catmull curve through rear, mid, and belly points so the tail root height lines up smoothly with the belly cross-section.

Now I'm thinking about color sectors on the dorsal clock — splitting back and belly regions into separate meshes that share edges at their boundaries, using angle ranges like [-70,70] for the back and [120,240] for the belly. For the dorsal fin, I'm mapping its rise from the dorsal start point near the hips up to the hip top, keeping the height gain modest.

For the fin membrane, I'm working out how to raise it slightly off the tube surface using offset lines along the normal, then considering whether a frilled or wavy outline would look better than a straight raised edge, since the back's height varies along the length of the body and needs to be accounted for when extruding the fin shape.

Still shaping the fin ripples...

For bone assignment, since the body bends between hips and chest, I'm thinking the rim should probably be split rather than rigidly tied to one bone — maybe build the outline in two halves so the rear portion near the tail can follow a different joint.

Working out the ripple pattern...

I'll skip smoothing and keep the zigzag sharp and chunky since the edges are far enough apart to avoid self-crossing, and the low-poly look is fine without rounding corners. Now I'm setting up the envelope calculation for the fin shape.

Checking the fin position near z=0.042, where it's near the head — but since the head geometry is handled separately, the fin surface there is fine. I'm also verifying the back-top sampling point lies exactly at the center of the back sector, and now working on the small ridge rods connecting each fin peak/valley to the base.

Deciding to include all 40 ridge rods on both sides, keeping the part budget near 80 after accounting for freckles and bulges. I'm working out rod placement—embedding them at x=±0.0018 within the 0.004 thickness, with bottom and top y-coordinates tied to the fin's rise, and tilting them slightly toward the back in z for a fanned look.

Now I'm placing shoulder and hip bulges as small skin-colored sphere mounds positioned just outside the body's surface width at those heights, sizing them around 0.016-0.017 radius to sit naturally against the torso.

But I realize the hip position at z=-0.06 might actually fall outside the body's rear taper, since the body narrows toward the tail root there — I may need to fatten the rear section slightly so the hip bulges stay flush against the surface rather than floating outside it.

Checking the rear cap placement against the tail root — the body's rounded cap at z=-0.056 with radius 0.03 bulges wider than the tail's radius 0.017 at z=-0.075, so there'll be a visible step where they meet. I'll adjust the end point to smooth that transition.

Now I'm converting the radius profile into a parametrized path, mapping z-position to t and interpolating smoothly between the key radius values. I'm also setting the vertical (ry) keys along the body so the top and bottom curves taper correctly from rear to front.

For the freckles, I'm scattering spots across the body surface using a filtered random distribution that keeps them on the upper, outward-facing areas while avoiding the fin region and staying within the body's z-range.

I'll filter freckles by distance from the four mound centers to avoid overlap, then work on a cloaca bump underneath the body using a ray hit and a small flattened sphere colored to stand out, possibly adding a darker slit detail. I'm also considering costal groove lines along the flanks using small rod shapes to mimic axolotl anatomy.

Adding flank groove details...

Adjusting the t-values to avoid the hip mound conflict, settling on four groove positions per side with slight angled offsets, thin sweep geometry, and a subtle dark pink tone for the lines.

I'm now assigning bone weights for the mounds by z-position—chest versus hips—and setting up skin/belly sector coloring with back and belly bands. For the sweep's bone list, I'm making sure both hips and chest joints are included since the path spans from rear to front, though I'm leaving the head joint out since it's not part of this particular part.

I'm now defining the rim sweep geometry—small polyline path along the zigzag top edge, thin radius to match fin thickness, rounded smooth skinning bound to a single joint—before moving into the extrude call parameters.

For the extrude, I'm setting the outline so the x-axis tracks the z-coordinate along the body and y tracks the vertical profile, building separate front and rear piece outlines at the 0.006 grid spacing, with the bottom edge sunk slightly inside the body surface to seat the fin properly.

Checking the rear fin height against the body's surface curvature near the hip cap, I'm noticing the computed height at z=-0.072 comes out around 0.076, which doesn't match the expected hipsTop value of 0.092 -- I need to reconcile that discrepancy.

I'll add an extra rise term that increases toward the rear using a smoothstep, pushing the peak height up near the tail so it meets the expected ~0.092 target at z=-0.072.

Writing taper and rod math...

I'll assume the Ctx type is already provided by the module and just use it in the function signature without importing it. Now I'm defining the body sweep profile, setting up key radius points along the z-axis for the torso cross-section and planning a smoothstep interpolation between them.

I'm checking that the shoulder and hip mound dimensions stay within the overall body silhouette's bounding box, adjusting the center offsets and scale factors at each point so they don't protrude past the guide boundary.

Now I'm working out the freckle surface sampling (limited to the body only), the cloaca placement via a downward ray hit on the belly with a flattened scaled sphere, and picking an appropriate skin-tone color for it.

Adding slit geometry...

Setting up the sweep call signature, then building the z-grid spanning rear to front sections with ridges assigned to hips bone for the rear and chest bone for the front, splitting at z=0. Noting the back sector skin edge detail, then finalizing the write.

I'm planning a function to construct the head and jaw geometry, keeping it robust and avoiding risky APIs by using simple scaled, bone-attached primitives, and I'll type the context loosely with `any` since the exact Ctx type isn't confirmed.

I'm working out the positions and dimensions for the skull and jaw ellipsoids, placing the head joint and jaw joint along the z-axis and calculating the y-range so the chin sits near the floor while the upper skull extends above it.

Adding a blunt snout ellipsoid and mounting a mouth-front point. Now I'm thinking about how to trace the mouth line as a seam curve across the face, trying to find surface points on the skull/jaw union so the lip path sits right on the surface rather than floating or clipping through it.

I need to guard against null hits from the outermost-surface query. For the smile shape, I'm tilting the mouth upward at the corners using elevation angles to create a cheek tuck, and adding cheek bulge spheres offset to the sides that push the silhouette outward slightly.

Checking the cheek bulge against the bounding box, I keep x within limits by tightening the sphere radius. But the skull taper near the back means the gill roots would end up floating outside the head surface at that z-depth, so I'm adding an extra ellipsoid mass at the back of the head to keep the gills anchored properly.

Now I'm splitting the skull into a main cranium ellipsoid plus a separate snout ellipsoid, adjusting their centers and radii so the z-ranges overlap correctly and stay within the 0.03 box minimum, then rechecking where the gill roots sit relative to the main skull surface at that depth.

Adding gill-bearing neck flank bulges with carefully tuned centers and radii so they stay just inside the box bounds, then switching to low-poly faceted spheres with flat shading for the part rendering, scaled per-axis for each bulge.

For the skull I'll settle on a slightly smoother sphere for a cuter look while keeping flat shading on smaller faceted pieces, then add a partial-sphere top cap slightly larger than the skull itself, oriented to sit over the crown without z-fighting.

Working through where the cap edge intersects the snout geometry to make sure the coverage lines up naturally at the forehead.

Checking the eye position against the skull surface math, the eye center lands right on the surface at about y=.099, so the eye bead will stick out roughly half its radius—exactly what I want for a protruding eye look.

I'm now working out how to orient the eye ring and eyelid pieces using the skull ellipsoid's surface normal at each point, so I can seat them flush against the curved skull rather than placing them flat. I'm thinking of writing a helper that queries the surface normal at a given point and uses it to orient embedded parts automatically.

I'm unsure whether the embed fraction sinks the geometry from its base or its center, so rather than guess I'll just write my own helper function that finds the nearest surface hit and positions parts explicitly myself.

Working out highlight placement: I want the highlight spheres offset from the bead's surface direction by blending the outward normal with an "up" and "side" tangent vector, biasing toward the midline so the highlights look consistent across beads.

For the eye bead itself, I'll keep it spherical rather than flattening it, and for brow bumps I'll position small scaled spheres just above the eye socket along the surface normal.

For blush discs on the cheeks, I'm setting up positions and radii for ellipsoid-shaped cheek highlights, scaling them thin along the normal direction and wider across the surface.
